passage:
First week of July. Irfan filled in the form for mechanical engineering. "Good jobs, good salary," he told his roommate Ujjwal. "Abbu will stop worrying." In his cupboard, under his shirts, was the old guitar he'd played since Class 8.
Five weeks later. Irfan sat through thermodynamics half asleep. He'd been up till two, playing guitar on the hostel roof. In the lab, he did the minimum. Ujjwal asked, "Do you even like engineering?" "I like what it'll give me," Irfan said. "Security. That matters." "And the guitar?" "That's just for me."
Three months later. Irfan joined the college band, two evenings a week. On other days he studied properly, even stayed back for a machine design doubt. "Engineering pays the rent," he said. "Music keeps me awake enough to do it." Both reasons were true, and he'd stopped pretending either one wasn't.

qa.q: Until what time was Irfan up playing guitar?
qa.a: He'd been up till two, playing guitar on the hostel roof.

qa.q: Why did Irfan choose engineering while loving music, and how did that feel at first?
qa.a: He wanted security and to ease Abbu's worry, but the pull toward music left him drained and half asleep, doing only the minimum.

qa.q: What helped Irfan bring more energy to both sides?
qa.a: Joining the college band two evenings a week and admitting both motives were real, which let him study properly on other days.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal see Irfan's change over the three months?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably noticed Irfan seeming more awake and settled once he stopped hiding his love for music.

grounding: Over three months a student who chose engineering for security while drawn to music admits both motives are real, and the tension shapes his energy.

passage: Yusuf, you want to know why I became a nurse when I loved singing? Let your Hansa Nani tell you. I was nineteen. My father had just lost his job at the mill. Nursing meant a stipend, a hostel, a job waiting at the end. Singing meant nothing but hope. So I chose nursing, and I told everyone it was my calling. But in the first year I was so tired and flat. I did my duties, but my heart wasn't in the ward. At night, in the hostel bathroom, I sang old songs to the tiles. One day the matron heard me and asked me to sing for the patients at the Christmas gathering. I sang, and an old man in bed six cried and held my hand. After that, something changed. The nursing was for the family, and the singing was for me, and both belonged in that ward.

qa.q: Why did nursing appeal to young Hansa's family situation?
qa.a: Her father had just lost his mill job, and nursing meant a stipend, a hostel and a job waiting at the end.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel in her first year of nursing?
qa.a: She felt tired and flat, doing her duties while her heart wasn't in the ward, because her love for singing had no place.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Hansa's energy?
qa.a: The matron asking her to sing for the patients at Christmas, which joined her two sets of reasons in the same ward.

qa.q: How might the old man in bed six have felt when Hansa sang?
qa.a: He was moved to tears and comforted, holding her hand as she sang.

grounding: A grandmother recalls choosing nursing for security while secretly loving singing, and how the tension shaped her energy until both found a place.

passage: The rain had flooded the road to the college, the electronics exam was at ten, and the tabla audition for the city youth festival was at four the same afternoon. Tanvir had chosen engineering for one reason he never hid: good jobs. His father drove an auto, and the family needed a steady salary. But tabla was the thing he thought about in every lecture. He waded through the water to the exam hall, wrote the paper quickly and well, then caught a crowded bus across town, his tabla wrapped in plastic. Parveen, who played sitar, met him at the gate. "You look half-dead." "Engineering in the morning, music in the evening," he grinned. "I need both." "Which one do you love?" He thought about it. "The music. But the engineering lets me keep it. Both are real." He played that afternoon with wet shoes, and better than he'd played all year.

qa.q: What time was the tabla audition?
qa.a: The tabla audition was at four the same afternoon.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel about his two reasons, engineering and music?
qa.a: Tanvir feels pulled both ways but settled in admitting both: engineering for security for his family, and music for love.

qa.q: What does Tanvir's day show about holding mixed motives?
qa.a: That when both reasons are admitted openly, he can give real energy to each, even on a hard, rainy day.

qa.q: How might Parveen see Tanvir's choice?
qa.a: Parveen seems curious and understanding, asking which he loves, and accepting that both matter.

grounding: On a flooded exam day a student who chose engineering for a salary and loves tabla holds both motives, which shapes his energy.

passage:
"Mohit, can you put your shoes on the rack?"
"What will I get?"
"Get?"
"A sticker? A chocolate?"
Anand put down his cup. "Mohit, why do you ask that every time?"
"Because you always give me something."
Anand thought of the chart on the fridge, full of stars. Bath: star. Brushing: star. Shoes: star.
"Okay. What if we try something new? You put the shoes on the rack, and then you tell me how the hallway looks."
Mohit sighed, then did it. "It looks tidy."
"How does that feel?"
"Nice. Nobody will fall."
"You thought of keeping people safe. That was thoughtful."
Mohit stood a little taller. "Can I do Papa's shoes too?"
"Go ahead."
Later that week, Anand took the star chart off the fridge, and kept just one small star for really hard days.

qa.q: What did Mohit ask when told to put his shoes on the rack?
qa.a: He asked, "What will I get?"

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when Mohit kept asking what he would get?
qa.a: Anand felt concerned, realising the star chart had taught Mohit to expect a prize for every small task.

qa.q: Which choice by Anand worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Mohit how the tidy hallway felt and naming his thoughtfulness, so the task felt meaningful instead of paid.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when he offers to do Papa's shoes too?
qa.a: Mohit seems proud and pleased, helping because it feels good, not for a prize.

grounding: A young parent notices his son asks for a prize before every chore and shifts to noticing effort and meaning, keeping rewards rare.

passage:
When Madhuri turned five, I started giving her a small toy for every chore. It worked like magic at first. She watered the plants, folded towels, put her toys away. Then one Sunday I asked her to help me carry the groceries and she folded her arms. "What will you give me?" I laughed, but it bothered me. The next day she asked again before feeding the fish, the fish she used to love feeding.
I realised I'd turned every little job into a trade. So I stopped the toys. Instead, I began saying what I noticed: "You carried the heavy bag all the way, that was strong." "The fish came up to see you." At first she sulked. After a week, she fed the fish without asking. She said, "They were hungry, Papa."
I still give a treat sometimes. But now it's a surprise, not a price.
— Kunal

qa.q: What did Madhuri used to love feeding?
qa.a: She used to love feeding the fish.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri's question about the groceries bother Kunal?
qa.a: Kunal felt uneasy and a little worried, seeing that toys for every chore had turned simple help into a trade.

qa.q: What did Kunal change, and why did it help?
qa.a: Kunal stopped the toys and started noticing effort and meaning aloud, so Madhuri helped because it mattered, not for a prize.

qa.q: What might Madhuri have felt when the toys stopped?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at first and sulked, then seemed to enjoy helping again for its own sake.

grounding: A young parent notices his daughter asks for a reward before every chore and shifts to noticing effort, using treats sparingly.

passage:
Note to myself, Sunday, by Saurabh (Kishore's father)
Kishore is six. Since the summer, I've paid him two rupees for every job: sweeping, watering, folding clothes. Today he wouldn't pass me the newspaper without asking, "How much?" He used to bring it running every morning, just to see me smile.
I've been watching him all week. He asks about money first, then does the job fast and badly. The joy has gone out of helping.
What I did next: I told him the paying is stopping, except for special big jobs. When he watered the tulsi this evening, I didn't give a coin. I said, "Look how the leaves are standing up. You did that." He crouched down and looked at the plant for a long time. Then he asked, "Can I water it tomorrow too?"

qa.q: How much has Saurabh been paying Kishore for each job?
qa.a: Two rupees for every job.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling as he watched Kishore all week?
qa.a: Saurabh felt sad and concerned that the joy had gone out of Kishore's helping.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that could bring the joy back?
qa.a: He stopped paying except for special big jobs and instead pointed out the real effect of Kishore's watering on the tulsi.

qa.q: How did Kishore seem to feel looking at the tulsi?
qa.a: Kishore seemed curious and proud, wanting to water it again tomorrow.

grounding: A young father notices his son asks for payment before every chore and shifts to noticing effort and meaning, keeping rewards for big jobs.

passage:
Supervisor's note, medical records unit, by Rukmini
Avni has been entering discharge summaries into the system for four months. It's repetitive work, and lately she's been slow and flat. Yesterday she said, "I'm just a typing machine. The salary is the only reason I'm here."
Today I asked her to sit with me while a doctor in the emergency room pulled up an old patient's record at 3 am. The doctor found the allergy note Avni had typed last month and changed the medicine because of it. Avni watched quietly.
Afterwards she said, "I didn't know anyone read them that carefully." I said, "Every line you enter is used by someone deciding what to do for a patient."
What I did next: I asked her to take the lead on checking allergy fields for the unit. This afternoon she was faster and more careful than I'd seen in weeks.

qa.q: What did the doctor find in the record Avni had typed?
qa.a: The doctor found the allergy note Avni had typed last month.

qa.q: How was Avni feeling about the work before the emergency-room visit?
qa.a: Avni felt flat and joyless, seeing herself as just a typing machine working only for the salary.

qa.q: Why did seeing the doctor use the record steady Avni's effort?
qa.a: It connected the dull task to something she values, patient safety, so the work felt meaningful as well as paid.

qa.q: What might Rukmini have noticed in Avni that afternoon?
qa.a: Rukmini noticed Avni was faster and more careful than in weeks.

grounding: A supervisor helps an adult in a joyless records job see how her work matters to patients, and meaning steadies her effort.

passage:
Thursday night
Six months at the call centre. Eight hours of the same script, the same complaints about bills. I only stay for the salary and the shift allowance. Today I nearly cried in the washroom.
Ganga called at dinner and asked, "Is there anything in it you actually like?" I said no. Then I thought for a while.
Actually, there is one thing. My English has changed. Six months ago I stammered with angry callers. Now I can calm them down in two sentences. Last week an old man said, "Madam, you explained it better than my son." I want to be a teacher one day, and I'm getting practice at explaining things to people who don't want to listen.
It doesn't make the job fun. But if I think of each call as practice for the classroom, maybe I can get through tomorrow.
Ankita

qa.q: How long has Ankita worked at the call centre?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel at work today, and why?
qa.a: Ankita felt worn down and close to tears, because the repetitive calls seemed to be only about the salary.

qa.q: What did Ankita find that could steady the effort?
qa.a: That each call builds a skill Ankita values, explaining things calmly, which is practice for becoming a teacher.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel hearing Ankita's answer?
qa.a: Ganga would probably feel relieved and encouraged that Ganga's question helped Ankita find some meaning.

grounding: An adult in a paid but joyless call centre job finds a part that builds a valued skill, which steadies effort without replacing pay.

passage:

Daycare note, monsoon week, by Thomas
Rain again. Time to go out to the covered play area. Yamini sat on the floor with her yellow gumboots. I offered help. She said, "No! Me do it!" and pulled the boot the wrong way round. passage:
"Avni, homework time."
"Nooo. I want to play."
Urmila sat down on the sofa. "Okay. You don't get to skip homework. But you get to choose. Five o'clock or six o'clock?"
Avni looked up. "I choose?"
"You choose."
"...Six. After cycling."
"Deal. And which first, maths or Hindi?"
"Hindi. It's shorter."
"Your call."
At six, Urmila didn't have to call her. Avni came in with her cheeks red from cycling, opened her Hindi book, and said, "I'm starting. I said six."
"You did," said Urmila.
"Tomorrow can I choose again?"
"Every day, between two times."
Avni grinned and started writing.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when Avni came in on her own?

grounding: A mother lets her daughter choose between two study times and which subject first, and small real choices increase cooperation.

passage:
The summer I was nine, Dida and I fought every afternoon over maths. One hot day, instead of calling me, Dida put two things on the table: my maths book and my English book. "You have to do both before the evening mango time. But you choose which one first, and whether you start at three or at four." I remember staring at her. Nobody had ever let me choose anything about homework. I chose English first, at four. At four o'clock I was at the table, before she even called. It felt like my plan, not her order. By the end of summer, I finished both most days without a single fight.
I still think of those two books on the table.
— Arnab

qa.q: What two books did Dida put on the table?
qa.a: The maths book and the English book.

qa.q: Why did Arnab come to the table at four before Dida even called?
qa.a: Arnab felt proud and in charge, because the plan felt like Arnab's own, not Dida's order.

qa.q: Why did Dida's two small choices end the daily fights?
qa.a: She kept the limit, both subjects before mango time, but gave real choices about order and time, so Arnab felt like an agent.

qa.q: How might Dida have felt when Arnab showed up on time?
qa.a: Dida probably felt relieved and pleased that the afternoon fights had stopped.

grounding: An adult recalls a grandmother letting them choose between two start times and which book first, which turned fights into cooperation.

passage:
Tutor's note, Christmas break, by Pallavi
Dhruv, age ten, fought every session last week. "I don't want to do science!" He'd kick the table leg until half the hour was gone.
This week I tried something different. I set out science and maths worksheets and said, "Both need doing today. You pick which first. And you pick: start now, or after a ten-minute snack?"
He narrowed his eyes. "Really?"
"Really."
He chose maths first, after the snack. At the ten-minute mark, he sat down on his own. No kicking. When he finished maths, he moved to science without being told.
What I did next: I'll keep offering two real choices at every session. He isn't choosing whether to work, only how. That seems to be enough.

qa.q: What did Dhruv choose to do first?
qa.a: He chose maths first, after the snack.

qa.q: What changed in how Dhruv felt when Pallavi offered choices?
qa.a: He seemed surprised and then more willing, feeling in control rather than ordered, so the kicking stopped.

qa.q: Why do Pallavi's two choices work inside a limit?
qa.a: Dhruv still has to do both worksheets, but choosing the order and start time makes him feel like an agent, not an object.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel after this session compared with last week?
qa.a: Pallavi was probably relieved and encouraged that the session went smoothly.

grounding: A tutor lets a boy choose which worksheet first and when to start, and small real choices within limits increase his cooperation.

passage:
Saturday
Mummy wrote my whole day on a sheet and stuck it on my door. 7:00 wake. 7:15 bath. 8:00 maths. 11:00 dance class. 1:00 lunch. Everything, even when to drink water.
I love dance class. I was waiting all week for it. But when I saw "11:00 dance class" on her sheet, something in me went hard. I said I had a headache. I didn't go.
Afreen called at noon. "Where were you? We learnt the new piece!" I felt sick. I wanted to be there so much.
I think it's this: it wasn't my plan any more. Even the thing I love felt like an order. And the only way to feel like me was to say no.
Which is so stupid, because I only hurt myself.
Maybe I'll ask Mummy if I can make my own sheet next week. She can check it.
Neelam

qa.q: What time was dance class on the sheet?
Why did Neelam skip the dance class even though Neelam loves it?
qa.a: Seeing it on Mummy's sheet made it feel like an order, and Neelam felt a threatened sense of ownership, so saying no felt like the only way to feel free.

qa.q: What is Neelam's idea for next week, and why might it help?
qa.a: To make Neelam's own sheet and let Mummy check it, which keeps the structure but gives back ownership.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt when Neelam didn't come?
qa.a: Afreen was probably surprised and a bit disappointed, since they learnt the new piece.

grounding: A teenager whose every step is scheduled refuses even a much-loved dance class, pushing back to protect a sense of ownership.

passage: In their small town near Satara, Anjali had become Mahima's timetable. Wake at six. Study at seven. Library at four, to read the English books Mahima loved. Every hour, Anjali checked. passage: The floodwater was knee-deep outside the district hospital, the power kept failing, and Payal and Hrithik were on their first night shift as nursing students. Payal had chosen nursing after a year of volunteering at a clinic, thinking hard about whether she could handle blood, nights, sadness. Hrithik's parents had chosen it for him because a cousin got a job abroad. By 3 am, both were soaked and exhausted. A generator failed and they held torches for the doctor. Hrithik kept checking his phone. "I didn't sign up for this." Payal was tired too; her feet ached and her uniform was muddy. But when an old woman squeezed her hand, she thought, This is what I chose. I knew it would be hard. At dawn, Hrithik said, "I'm thinking of quitting." Payal, rubbing her eyes, said, "I'm thinking of breakfast. And coming back tomorrow."

qa.q: How deep was the floodwater outside the hospital?
qa.a: It was knee-deep.

qa.q: How did Payal feel through the hard night, and what kept her going?
qa.a: Payal was exhausted and aching but steady, because she had chosen nursing after real reflection and knew it would be hard.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do to find his own reasons for staying or leaving?
qa.a: He could take time to reflect on what he wants, perhaps by talking to a mentor, rather than staying only because his parents chose it.

qa.q: How might the old woman who squeezed Payal's hand have felt?
qa.a: She probably felt comforted and grateful for Payal's care during the frightening flood night.

grounding: On a flooded first night shift, a nursing student who chose her path after reflection holds up better than a classmate pushed into it.

passage: Saurabh had spent a year after school working on his uncle's farm near Nagpur before choosing agricultural science. He'd asked farmers what they needed, read about soil, and decided. Saurabh was upset too; he'd studied hard for that practical. But he said, "I know why I'm doing mine. Uncle's cotton crop failed because the soil was wrong. I want to fix that." qa.q: How did Saurabh feel after failing, and what kept him going?
qa.a: Saurabh was upset because he'd studied hard, but his own reason, fixing soil for farmers like his uncle, gave him the will to go straight back to the lab.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do to find her footing after this setback?

"Kamal, you failed the jury. Aren't you going to quit?"
"No, Manoj. I'm redoing the sculpture."
"But it's so much work. And your parents wanted you to do commerce."
"I know. I spent a whole year thinking about it before I chose fine arts. I visited three art colleges, I worked at a potter's shop. I knew it would be hard."
"And it's hard."
"Really hard. I cried after the jury."
"So?"
"So I chose this. It's mine. When it's hard, I remember why."
"I'm in engineering because Papa said so. Every time something goes wrong, I just want to leave."
"Maybe that's the difference."
"What?"
"You didn't choose it. It's hard to hold on to something that isn't yours."
Manoj was quiet. Then: "Show me the sculpture."
"It's only half-done."
"Show me anyway."

passage: Vinita had joined the small NGO in Kurukshetra full of ideas for the girls' literacy centre. But her supervisor, Hemant, checked everything. Which chalk to buy. How to arrange the benches. Which story to read on Tuesday. When she planned a spelling game, he changed it to a worksheet. After three months, Vinita stopped suggesting things. She came at nine, followed the list, and left at five. The girls noticed. "Didi, you don't laugh any more." One evening, Vinita stayed back and knocked on Hemant's door. "Sir, can I ask something? Could you tell me what you want the girls to achieve by March, and let me decide how to teach it? You can check the results every month." Hemant frowned, then nodded slowly. "Reading two-letter words, all of them. By March." "Okay." The next week, she brought back the spelling game. The girls laughed so loudly Hemant came to the door. He watched, and didn't change anything.

passage: In the Toronto warehouse, Bilal had been the one who spotted problems and fixed them before anyone asked. Then Tariq became shift manager. Tariq checked every pallet Bilal loaded, reorganised shelves Bilal had arranged, and asked for a report after every hour. Within a month, Bilal stopped noticing the loose labels and the leaking boxes. He did exactly what the checklist said and nothing else. At the end of his shift, he felt emptier than when he'd worked double hours. One Friday, a truck left with a wrong delivery Bilal had seen coming but not flagged. Tariq was furious. Bilal said quietly, "I didn't think it was my job to think any more." Tariq stopped. After a long pause, he said, "What if I tell you the targets for the week, and you decide how to run your section?" Bilal nodded. By the next Friday, he'd flagged three problems before they happened.

qa.q: How often did Tariq ask Bilal for a report?
qa.a: After every hour.

qa.q: How did Bilal feel at the end of his shifts under Tariq's checking?
qa.a: Bilal felt empty and drained, more than after double hours, because he had no room left for his own judgement.

qa.q: What did Tariq offer that brought back Bilal's initiative?
qa.a: Clear weekly targets with freedom for Bilal to decide how to run his section.

qa.a: Tariq seemed shocked into silence, realising his checking had switched off Bilal's initiative.

passage:
The summer I was ten, fractions beat me every day. Pranav bhaiya would give me a sum, and I'd get it wrong. Again. Again. After two weeks I said, "I can't do maths. I'm just bad at it." I stopped trying. When he gave me a sum, I'd write any answer just to finish.
Then one afternoon he did something new. He cut a roti into four pieces and asked me to give him one quarter. Easy. Then two quarters. "That's a half," I said. He grinned. "You just did fractions." The next day, a pizza drawing with eighths. I got it right. And the next. Each small win made me want to try the next one.
I wasn't bad at maths. I'd just never felt myself get better at it.
— Shreya

qa.a: He cut a roti into four pieces.

qa.a: He used a roti and drawings to give easy, winnable steps, so Shreya could feel improvement and want to try again.

qa.q: How might Pranav bhaiya have felt when Shreya said "That's a half"?
qa.a: He was probably happy and relieved to see Shreya succeed.

grounding: A child recalls failing at fractions until deciding maths was impossible, and how small experiences of getting better restored motivation.

Class teacher's note, Onam week, by Jomon
Gargi, Class 4, has failed four fraction tests in a row. Today, while the others made pookalam designs, her maths book stayed closed. "I'm stupid at maths," she said. "Why try?" She didn't even write her name on the worksheet.

passage:
Diwali holidays, Tuesday
Jaya didi tried to help me with fractions again. I got the first three wrong. So I closed the book and said, "Forget it. I can't do maths. I'm too dumb."
Didi didn't argue. She took the box of sweets Nani sent and put it on the table. "There are twelve kaju katlis. If you get one third, how many?" I counted. "Four." "Correct. You just did a fraction." I laughed. Then she asked for one quarter. Three. Right again.
I got eight right in a row, and ate one sweet for each.
I still hate the book. But I think maybe I'm not dumb. I think I just never got enough right to feel it.
Tomorrow Didi said we'll do it with the diyas.
Nilesh
